title: Instrumentation to study myofibril mechanics from static to artificial simulations of cardiac cycle
author: Vikhorev, Ferenczi, et al.
materials: A small volume (10–30 μL) of myofibril solution was pipetted onto a coverslip of a custom made temperature-controlled bath chamber, which was positioned on the microscope stage. The bath chamber was made of anodized aluminum with water circulation flow channels for additional temperature control using a thermostatic water bath circulator. The bath chamber had a round hole in the center that was closed by a coverslip. After myofibrils were added, the bath chamber was filled with relaxing solution supplemented with the above mentioned protease inhibitors. Most of the myofibrils slightly adhered to the coverslip. Using two specially prepared fine glass microtools, each mounted onto a micromanipulator, a selected myofibril or small bundle were picked up and positioned horizontally.

Despite improvements in performance of spreadsheet and commercial statistical software in recent years, they are usually not effective for processing large data sets. Data analysis software was written in LabVIEW to visualize the acquired data, to process it, to fit model curves to key components, to visualize the results and to organize them for further analysis. The data analysis software (Fig. 4) is loaded with saved experimental data. The tension traces are automatically identified, numbered and activation and relaxation events are automatically and accurately selected. The valve configuration and therefore which activating solution is used for each contractile event is automatically determined. The transition between the slow relaxation phase and the fast relaxation phase, and the segment of the slow phase which is to be fitted with a straight line is selected manually using cursors. After calibration parameters are applied, the trace segment is fitted with a single exponential. The fitting intervals can be easily adjusted with the cursors with constant visual feedback. The best-fit parameters are saved and transferred to another statistical program for further analysis.

steps.title: Isolate myofibrils from tissue
steps.instruction: Take 1–3 small muscle pieces (total 2–5 mg, can be as low as 1 mg) frozen in liquid nitrogen and place them in a 2 mL LoBind Eppendorf tube containing ice‑cold permeabilisation solution (10 mM Tris pH 7.1, 132 mM NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl₂, 5 mM EGTA, 5 mM DTT, 10 mM NaN₃, 20 mM BDM, 1 % peroxide‑ and carbonyl‑free Triton X‑100). Add protease inhibitors: chymostatin 10 µM, pepstatin 5 µM, leupeptin 10 µM (or 40 µM; use 40 mM if the myofibrils will be used for mechanical studies), E‑64 10 µM, PMSF 200 µM. Shake on ice with slight agitation for 3 h. Remove the solution, wash the permeabilised sample by incubating 15 min in washing solution (same composition but without Triton X‑100 and BDM). Homogenise for 15 s with an Ultra‑Turrax T8 (speed setting 5, S8N‑5G, IKA Werke GmbH & Co., Staufen, Germany). Let the suspension sit on ice 5 min to allow myofibrils to settle, then pellet by low‑speed centrifugation (MSE Micro Centaur, Sanyo, UK) for 1–2 min. Pipette off the supernatant, add 300 µL fresh washing solution, resuspend the pellet by gentle pipetting and keep on ice for up to 5 days.

substeps.instruction: Weigh 1–3 muscle pieces (1–5 mg total).
Add to 2 mL tube with permeabilisation solution (composition listed).
Add protease inhibitors (concentrations listed).
Shake on ice 3 h.
Remove solution and wash 15 min in washing solution.
Homogenise 15 s with Ultra‑Turrax T8 (speed 5).
Incubate on ice 5 min.
Centrifuge low speed 1–2 min.
Remove supernatant, add 300 µL washing solution, resuspend, store on ice ≤5 days.

steps.title: Mount myofibrils in temperature‑controlled chamber
steps.instruction: Pipette 10–30 µL of the myofibril suspension onto the coverslip of a custom anodized‑aluminum bath chamber (water‑circulation channels, thermostatic water‑bath circulator, round central hole sealed by the coverslip) positioned on the microscope stage. Fill the chamber with relaxing solution containing the same protease inhibitors as above; most myofibrils will adhere slightly to the coverslip. Using two fine glass microtools mounted on micromanipulators, pick a single myofibril or a small bundle and position it horizontally.

substeps.instruction: Place 10–30 µL myofibril solution on coverslip.
Fill chamber with relaxing solution + protease inhibitors.
Allow myofibrils to adhere.
Pick and position a myofibril with two glass microtools.

steps.title: Prepare glass microtools
steps.instruction: Pull borosilicate capillary glass (1 mm outer diameter) with a Narishige PC‑10 pipette puller and shape with a Narishige MF‑900 microforge. For the L‑shaped cantilever force probe, pull to obtain a tip ≥1.5 mm long with a constant diameter of 10–12 µm, cut off excess glass, close the open end by heating, then bend to a right angle 1.2–1.5 mm from the tip to create a strain‑sensitive cantilever. For the stiff microtool, pull to a tip ≈10 µm with a short taper; keep it straight. Mount the stiff tool on a piezo actuator on the left side of the chamber to control myofibril length.

substeps.instruction: Pull capillary with PC‑10.
Shape with MF‑900.
Create L‑shaped cantilever (tip ≥1.5 mm, 10–12 µm diameter, bend 1.2–1.5 mm from tip).
Close open end by heating.
Create stiff microtool (tip ≈10 µm, short taper).
Mount stiff tool on left‑side piezo actuator.

steps.title: Blacken cantilever tip region
steps.instruction: Position the L‑shaped cantilever vertically at a distance of about 70–90 µm from the heating wire of the microforge. Apply high heat; the platinum oxide from the heater wire deposits on the relatively cold glass, blackening the region from the tip to the bend over several seconds.

substeps.instruction: Place cantilever 70–90 µm from heating wire.
Turn on high heat for a few seconds.
Allow platinum oxide deposition to blacken tip‑to‑bend region.

steps.title: Run contraction experiments
steps.instruction: Maintain the bath solution level throughout the experiment using an Instech P720 peristaltic pump (Harvard Apparatus, USA) in suction mode. Perform all measurements in a temperature‑controlled room set to 17 °C.

substeps.instruction: Set peristaltic pump to suction mode to keep solution level constant.
Conduct experiments at 17 °C.

steps.title: Load and preprocess experimental data
steps.instruction: Open the previously saved acquisition files in the LabVIEW analysis program. The software reads the metadata, automatically identifies Ca²⁺ transients, determines the activating [Ca²⁺] from the valve position, numbers each contraction‑relaxation cycle, and separates activation and relaxation phases.

steps.title: Fit force traces and extract tension
steps.instruction: Apply calibration parameters, then for each trace segment fit either a single exponential or a linear model using the visual‑feedback interface. Manually select the boundary between the slow and fast relaxation phases and the portion of the slow phase to be fitted linearly using cursors. Calculate maximal tension as the difference between the baseline and the exponential plateau.

substeps.instruction: Apply calibration.
Fit exponential or linear model with visual feedback.
Manually set edge between slow and fast relaxation.
Select linear segment of slow phase.
Compute maximal tension (baseline‑to‑plateau).

steps.title: Calculate rate constants
steps.instruction: From the exponential fit obtain the activation rate constant k_ACT and the fast‑relaxation rate constant k_REL. From the linear fit obtain the slope; compute the slow‑phase rate constant k_LIN as k_LIN = –slope × y_max (normalised to the maximum tension).

steps.title: Fit Hill equation and perform statistics
steps.instruction: Fit the relationship between maximal tension and [Ca²⁺] with the Hill equation F = F_max · [Ca²⁺]^nH / (EC50^nH + [Ca²⁺]^nH) using GraphPad Prism 6. Extract EC50 and the Hill coefficient n_H. Perform unpaired t‑tests for group comparisons and generate graphs in Prism.

steps.title: Export fitted parameters
steps.instruction: Save all best‑fit parameters from the LabVIEW software and transfer them to a statistical program for further analysis and figure preparation.
